opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core challenge with Genie was that we wanted to learn a generative interactive environment purely from video, with no action labels, and video is really expensive to model. If you treat every pixel in every frame independently, the sequence lengths blow up very quickly, especially once you want to generate many frames autoregressively. So we needed a compact discrete representation that the dynamics model and the latent action model could work with.

The reason we went spatiotemporal rather than just encoding each frame on its own is that a lot of what makes video coherent is in the temporal relationships: how objects move, what stays consistent from frame to frame. A purely spatial tokenizer, like a standard VQ-VAE applied per frame, throws that context away at the tokenization stage, and then the downstream model has to recover it. With the spatiotemporal approach, the tokens for a given frame are informed by the frames before it, so the representation already carries some of that dynamics information. In our experiments that gave better video quality and better controllability than a spatial-only tokenizer.

The other piece was efficiency. We built it on a memory-efficient ST-transformer, which interleaves spatial attention within a frame with temporal attention across time steps, instead of doing full attention over every token in the whole clip. That makes compute scale roughly linearly with the number of frames rather than quadratically, which mattered a lot because we were training at scale on a large corpus of internet gameplay videos. We also made the temporal attention causal, which fits how the model is actually used: you generate the next frame conditioned on the past and on the latent action the user picks.

So it came down to a trade-off. We wanted tokens that captured motion and temporal consistency, but that were still cheap enough to train on a lot of video and to roll out interactively. The spatiotemporal tokenizer gave us both, and it ended up being an important part of what made the whole system work.

r002.rationale: It explains that spatiotemporal tokens use prior frames to carry motion and temporal consistency, while spatial-only tokenization loses that context needed by downstream next-frame generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question we thought about a lot. When you're working with video, you have this huge amount of data—every frame is a bunch of pixels, and if you tried to feed raw pixels into a transformer the sequence length just explodes. So you need some kind of compression, and tokenization is the standard way of doing that. The question is really what you compress over.

A lot of prior work would tokenize each frame independently, so you're basically running an image tokenizer frame by frame. The problem with that is video has a lot of temporal redundancy. Consecutive frames look very similar, and if you tokenize them independently you're spending capacity re-encoding the same background over and over, and you're not actually capturing the thing we care about, which is how things change over time.

So for Genie we used an ST-ViViT style encoder—a spatiotemporal transformer—where the tokenizer sees a window of frames and can attend across both space and time. That lets the tokens encode motion and dynamics, not just static appearance. And that turned out to matter a lot downstream, because the whole point of Genie is that the dynamics model has to predict the next frame conditioned on an action. If the tokens already carry temporal information, that prediction becomes much easier and the resulting videos are more coherent.

We did also find it was more compute efficient. We compared against a per-frame approach and against a full 3D convolution style encoder, and the spatiotemporal transformer gave us better reconstructions for a similar token budget. One detail that was important is that we made the tokenizer causal in time, so when you're generating a new frame you only depend on past frames. That lines up with how the model is actually used at inference, where you're generating step by step as a player takes actions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compressing video into tokens and says temporal information improves coherence, but it does not attribute sharper generations to predicting discrete patch tokens instead of pixels directly.

r002.rationale: It explains that per-frame tokenization misses temporal redundancy and change, while spatiotemporal tokens capture motion and dynamics that help the model predict the next frame.

astra-6.text:
We chose a spatiotemporal tokenizer because we wanted a compact representation that captures both what’s in a frame and how things change over time. If you tokenize each frame independently, you’re not taking advantage of the redundancy between frames, and motion becomes something the dynamics model has to infer from those separate representations.

With spatiotemporal tokenization, we can use that temporal structure to represent the video more efficiently. That matters for Genie because we’re learning to generate future frames in response to actions, so preserving the information about how the scene evolves is really important. We also use causal temporal attention, so the representation at a given point doesn’t look ahead into future frames. That keeps it consistent with how we generate video, one step at a time.

r002.rationale: It explains that frame-by-frame tokenization misses temporal redundancy and leaves motion for the model to infer, while spatiotemporal tokenization preserves how the scene changes for future-frame generation.

sol-6.1.text: We chose spatiotemporal tokenization because Genie needs to learn how a world changes over time, not just what individual frames look like. There’s a lot of redundancy between consecutive frames, so processing them jointly lets us compress the video into a much smaller sequence of discrete tokens while preserving information about motion. That makes the dynamics model much more efficient to train. We also use causal temporal attention, so the representation of a frame can depend on previous frames but can’t look into the future, which is important when you want to generate the world one step at a time.

r002.rationale: It explains that the representation captures how the world changes over time rather than only individual-frame appearance, and connects this to generating the world one step at a time.
